metadata.title: Exhaustive Catalogue of Pitch-Hue Mapping Systems Across History and Cultures
metadata.description: Over 50 color-music mapping systems beyond the 15 already collected in the existing dataset, organized chronologically within traditions. Compiled for the Tsinghua University thesis on crossmodal correspondences.
metadata.compiledFor: Alex Noah Feldman, Master's Thesis, Tsinghua University SIGS

threeParadigms.linear_spectral: Maps the chromatic scale directly onto the visible spectrum, C=red ascending to B=violet (Mizler, Jameson, Bishop, Klein, Belmont, Boomwhackers)
threeParadigms.circle_of_fifths: Maps tonal relationships onto a color wheel so harmonically related keys are chromatically adjacent (Scriabin, Jack Ox)
threeParadigms.cosmological: Embeds pitch-color in a larger system of elemental correspondences (Chinese wuxing, Indian svara, Al-Kindi, Kircher)

metadata.keyEmpiricalConclusion: No specific pitch-to-hue mapping has been validated at the population level. The only robust crossmodal correspondence is pitch-to-lightness (higher = lighter), confirmed across cultures, ages, and even species.

systems.name: Ancient Persian System
systems.author: Unknown
systems.AdditionalComment: One of the earliest documented tone-color schemes. Assigns seven diatonic notes to colors without spectral logic. Theoretical basis unknown but likely cosmological.

systems.name: Chinese Wuxing Five-Tone/Five-Color System (五音五色)
systems.author: Traditional Chinese cosmology
systems.source: Zuo Zhuan, Liji, Lüshi Chunqiu, Huainanzi, Huangdi Neijing
systems.AdditionalComment: The most robustly documented non-Western pitch-color system. The Huangdi Neijing extends this into medical theory: 宫声入脾, 商声入肺, 角声入肝, 徵声入心, 羽声入肾. Zhu Zaiyu (朱载堉) independently derived 12-tone equal temperament in 1584, but no classical or modern Chinese scholar has systematically extended the five-color mapping to all twelve lǜ (律). The seven additional tones were considered 偏音 (biased tones) and excluded from the five-element framework. This gap represents a potential original contribution for a thesis at Tsinghua.

systems.name: Aristotle / Cureau de la Chambre Interval System
systems.author: Aristotle, transmitted by Marin Cureau de la Chambre
systems.AdditionalComment: Maps musical intervals — not individual pitches — to colors on a white-to-black brightness scale. Represents a fundamentally different paradigm from later pitch-class systems.

systems.name: Indian Navarasa Color System
systems.author: Bharata Muni
systems.AdditionalComment: Assigns colors to nine aesthetic sentiments (rasa) which connect to ragas through emotional expression. Śānta was added by Abhinavagupta (~10th century). The Sanskrit root 'raga' itself means 'color' or 'to dye'. This is an emotion-mediated system rather than a direct pitch-to-hue mapping.

systems.name: Indian Svara-to-Color Associations
systems.author: Traditional, codified by Śārṅgadeva
systems.AdditionalComment: Seven svaras carry color and planetary associations across multiple teaching traditions. These vary between Hindustani and Carnatic systems and are less uniformly codified than the Chinese wuxing correspondences.

systems.name: Al-Kindi's Cosmological Oud-String System
systems.author: Al-Kindi
systems.source: Risala fi'l-Luhun wa'n-Nagham; Adam Bursi, Islamic Sensory History (Brill, 2024)
systems.AdditionalComment: Four-element framework reflecting Greco-Arabic philosophy rather than the Chinese quinary system. The Ikhwan al-Safa (Brethren of Purity, ~10th century) continued this tradition in their Rasa'il, Epistle 5 on Music.

systems.name: Rudolph of Saint Trond Modal Colors
systems.author: Rudolph of Saint Trond
systems.AdditionalComment: One of the earliest medieval Western modal-color systems.

systems.name: Franchino Gaffurio Modal Colors
systems.author: Franchino Gaffurio
systems.AdditionalComment: Modal colors from Gaffurio's Renaissance theoretical writings.

systems.name: Gioseffo Zarlino Interval-Color System
systems.author: Gioseffo Zarlino
systems.AdditionalComment: Renaissance interval-to-color system.

systems.name: Girolamo Cardanus Interval-Color System
systems.author: Girolamo Cardanus
systems.AdditionalComment: A different interval-to-color scheme from Zarlino's. Both are Renaissance systems mapping intervals rather than individual pitch classes.

systems.name: Athanasius Kircher Interval-Color System
systems.author: Athanasius Kircher
systems.AdditionalComment: Kircher mapped intervals (not individual pitches) to colors within a cosmological framework linking music, color, elements, and planets.

systems.name: David Gottlob Diez Note-Color-Planet System
systems.author: David Gottlob Diez
systems.AdditionalComment: A note-color-planet system combining chromatic pitch-class mapping with astrological associations.

systems.name: Lorenz Christoph Mizler Newtonian System
systems.author: Lorenz Christoph Mizler
systems.AdditionalComment: A direct response to Newton, mapping seven notes to Newton's seven spectral colors ascending from C. This is the simplest possible Newtonian mapping and was later duplicated by Sudre's Solresol.

systems.name: Johann Gottlob Krüger System
systems.author: Johann Gottlob Krüger
systems.AdditionalComment: A variation on Newton's spectral mapping.

systems.name: Leonhard Euler System
systems.author: Leonhard Euler
systems.AdditionalComment: Unusually, Euler placed purple at C rather than red. He essentially rejected the color-tone analogy as scientifically meaningful despite contributing this table.

systems.name: Louis François Henri Lefébure System
systems.author: Louis François Henri Lefébure
systems.AdditionalComment: A modified Castel system with a strikingly different arrangement from other Newtonian-era systems.

systems.name: Georg Tobias Ludwig Sachs (First Documented Synesthete)
systems.author: Georg Tobias Ludwig Sachs
systems.source: Sachs (1812, Latin doctoral dissertation); Jewanski, Day, and Ward (2009), Journal of the History of the Neurosciences
systems.AdditionalComment: The first documented synesthete in history. His tone-color experiences were mediated by letter-name associations: musical tones inherited the colors of their German letter designations.

systems.name: D.D. Jameson Chromatic Spectral Mapping
systems.author: D.D. Jameson
systems.source: Colour-Music, Smith Elder and Co., London, p. 12
systems.AdditionalComment: A full 12-note chromatic mapping representing the linear-spectral paradigm. Jameson built an instrument passing light through colored liquids.

systems.name: Charles Fourier Inverted Spectral System
systems.author: Charles Fourier
systems.AdditionalComment: An inverted spectral mapping — reverses the direction of Newton/Mizler by placing violet at C and red at B.

systems.name: François Sudre / Solresol System
systems.author: François Sudre
systems.AdditionalComment: Identical to Mizler's Newtonian mapping, used for Sudre's universal language Solresol where colors served as one of multiple modalities for communication.

systems.name: T. Seemann 12-Note System
systems.author: T. Seemann
systems.AdditionalComment: A 12-note system with an unusual endpoint: B = black rather than a spectral hue.

systems.name: Bleuler and Lehmann Synesthesia Survey
systems.author: Eugen Bleuler and Karl Lehmann
systems.source: Zwangsmässige Lichtempfindungen durch Schall, Leipzig: Fues (1881)

keyFindings.mainFinding: Higher pitches mapped to lighter/brighter colors. Pitch-to-brightness, not pitch-to-hue.

systems.AdditionalComment: The first large-scale synesthesia survey. Documented a connection between pitch and brightness — higher pitches mapped to lighter/brighter colors. This finding has been replicated consistently for 145 years.

systems.name: Bainbridge Bishop Color Organ Spectral System
systems.author: Bainbridge Bishop
systems.source: A Souvenir of the Color Organ (1893)
systems.AdditionalComment: Bishop built at least three color organs (all destroyed by fire; one owned by P.T. Barnum). He believed this was 'correct according to nature as displayed by rainbows.'

systems.name: Théodore Flournoy Synesthesia Cases
systems.author: Théodore Flournoy
systems.AdditionalComment: The most extensive 19th-century treatment of synesthesia, including cases of audition colorée. Flournoy introduced the inducer/concurrent distinction and classified synesthetes as 'projectors' versus 'associators' — concepts rediscovered a century later by Dixon, Smilek, and Merikle (2004). Contains qualitative case descriptions rather than aggregate mapping tables. Remains untranslated from French.

systems.name: Helena Blavatsky / Theosophical System
systems.author: Helena Blavatsky
systems.AdditionalComment: A Theosophical mapping that influenced Scriabin. Sol = black is an unusual assignment. Published in Isis Unveiled and The Secret Doctrine.

systems.name: Rosicrucian Order System
systems.author: Rosicrucian Order (attributed)
systems.source: Esoteric circles; possibly speculative attribution to Berlioz, Debussy, Wagner
systems.AdditionalComment: Attributed to esoteric circles associated (possibly speculatively) with Berlioz, Debussy, and Wagner. Uses a just-intonation frequency basis. Starts spectral mapping from G rather than C.

systems.name: Amy Beach Synesthetic Key-Colors
systems.author: Amy Beach
systems.AdditionalComment: A confirmed synesthete with involuntary key-color associations. These are synesthetic percepts, not a theoretical system.

systems.name: Leonid Sabaneyev Documentation of Scriabin
systems.author: Leonid Sabaneyev (documenting Alexander Scriabin)
systems.AdditionalComment: Sabaneyev documented and published Scriabin's color system in the Moscow journal Muzyka in January 1911, two months before the Prometheus premiere. He noted that 'originally [Scriabin] recognized clearly no more than three colors — red, yellow, and blue, corresponding to C, D, and F-sharp respectively.' Multiple synesthesia researchers (Harrison 2001; Cytowic and Eagleman 2009; Dann 1998) have questioned whether Scriabin was a genuine synesthete, noting his system follows the circle of fifths mapped to the spectrum — suggesting deliberate construction rather than involuntary perception. The Scriabin Museum archives contain multiple different versions in his own hand.

systems.name: Wassily Kandinsky Timbre-Color System
systems.author: Wassily Kandinsky
systems.AdditionalComment: Kandinsky mapped colors to timbres and registers, not pitch classes. His system is explicitly about 'inner necessity' and spiritual vibration, influenced by Goethe and Wagner. This represents a fundamentally different approach from pitch-to-hue mappings.

systems.name: Roy de Maistre Spectral System
systems.author: Roy de Maistre
systems.AdditionalComment: Australian painter who exhibited a spectral mapping starting from A rather than C.

systems.name: Leon Theremin / Illumovox Continuous System
systems.author: Leon Theremin
systems.AdditionalComment: A continuous (not discrete) spectrum mapping for the Illumovox instrument. Lowest pitches = dark red, ascending smoothly through the spectrum to highest pitches approaching ultraviolet.

systems.name: Adrian Bernard Klein Spectroscope System
systems.author: Adrian Bernard Klein
systems.source: Colour-Music: The Art of Light (1926), p. 209
systems.AdditionalComment: A linear spectral mapping using a large spectroscope to project spectral light.

systems.name: Artists Who Explicitly Rejected Fixed Pitch-Color Mappings
systems.author: Thomas Wilfred, Mary Hallock Greenewalt, Alexander László, Vladimir Baranoff-Rossiné

rejectionDetails.Thomas Wilfred (Clavilux, 1919\u20131960: Organized Lumia art around color, form, and motion as independent dimensions; preferred silent exhibitions.
rejectionDetails.Mary Hallock Greenewalt (Sarabet/Nourath: Used alternating and merging colors expressively rather than systematically.
rejectionDetails.Alexander L\u00e1szl\u00f3 (Sonchromatos: Explicitly rejected 'individual keys illustrated by clearly related colors' in favor of expressive unity.
rejectionDetails.Vladimir Baranoff-Rossin\u00e9 (Optophon: Reversed direction entirely: light passed through painted glass discs, photoelectric cell converted opacity variations into pitch (color→sound).

systems.AdditionalComment: Several major color-music practitioners deliberately avoided static pitch-color correspondence. This is itself a significant finding for the thesis — the rejection of fixed mappings by practicing artists suggests that creative practice resists the systematization that theorists seek.

systems.name: I.J. Belmont Equal-Division Spectral System
systems.author: I.J. Belmont
systems.source: The Modern Dilemma in Art (1944); also Wyschnegradsky (1979)
systems.AdditionalComment: An equal-division spectral mapping. Ivan Wyschnegradsky proposed a nearly identical scale in 1979.

systems.name: August Aeppli Diatonic System
systems.author: August Aeppli
systems.source: Gerstner, The Forms of Color (1986), p. 169
systems.AdditionalComment: An 8-note diatonic mapping including the octave C.

systems.name: Galeyev-Vanechkina / Prometei Institute Schema
systems.author: Bulat Galeyev and Irina Vanechkina
systems.source: Prometei Institute, Kazan; Dover/Eulenberg editions of Scriabin's Prometheus
systems.AdditionalComment: The Galeyev-Vanechkina 'Musico-Chromo-Logo Schema' was constructed for modern published editions of Scriabin's Prometheus (Dover, Eulenberg). It correlates major keys on the circle of fifths with color designations, closely following Sabaneyev's 1911 table. As Gawboy and Townsend demonstrated in Music Theory Online (2012), this schema was created before the rediscovery of Scriabin's own annotated 1913 Parisian manuscript and may not accurately represent Scriabin's actual compositional practice.

systems.name: Steve Zieverink Physical Wavelength Transposition
systems.author: Steve Zieverink
systems.source: Twelve + Twelve (2004); Contemporary Arts Center, Cincinnati
systems.AdditionalComment: A physical-wavelength system produced by doubling sound frequency 40 octaves into the light range. Results differ markedly from spectral systems because the frequency ratio between C4 and C5 (2:1) does not map linearly onto the visible spectrum.

systems.name: Jack Ox Virtual Color Organ
systems.author: Jack Ox
systems.AdditionalComment: Ox superimposes a 12-step color wheel over the circle of fifths: as music modulates through keys, the same pattern occurs as movement through colors. Minor keys are represented on an inner wheel, three steps behind major keys. Her timbre system uses over 130 RGB color mixtures where instrument families are represented by graduated color sets, further modified by mutes and playing techniques.

systems.name: Katherine Lubar Itten Color Wheel Application
systems.author: Katherine Lubar
systems.AdditionalComment: Applied Johannes Itten's 12-step color wheel to create color intervals analogous to musical consonance and dissonance, rather than mapping individual pitches to colors.

systems.name: Japanese Gogyo (五行) Adopted Wuxing System
systems.author: Adopted from Chinese tradition
systems.source: Adopted via Baekje; gagaku court music tradition
systems.AdditionalComment: Japan adopted the Chinese Wuxing system (called gogyo 五行) via Baekje in the 6th century CE. The five directional colors (goshiki 五色) map implicitly onto gagaku court music's pentatonic scales derived from Chinese theory. Prince Shōtoku's Twelve Level Cap and Rank System (冠位十二階, 603 CE) used these five colors with light/dark variants. No uniquely Japanese pitch-color system independent of the Chinese framework has been documented.

systems.name: Korean Ohaeng (오행) Adopted Wuxing System
systems.author: Adopted from Chinese tradition
systems.AdditionalComment: Korea adopted the Chinese system as ohaeng (오행), with the identical obangsaek (오방색) five-directional color scheme. Korean court music (aak/아악) directly imported Chinese yayue ritual music and its five-element correspondences. Korean folk traditions (pansori, sanjo) emphasize emotional expression over cosmological correspondence.

systems.name: Lawrence Marks Pitch-Brightness Correspondence
systems.author: Lawrence Marks

keyFindings.mainFinding: Brighter colors associate with higher pitches, darker with lower. Documented in both synesthetes and non-synesthetes.

systems.AdditionalComment: Established the foundational pitch-brightness correspondence. This is the most robust crossmodal finding in the literature.

systems.name: Timothy Hubbard Pitch-Lightness Study
systems.author: Timothy Hubbard

keyFindings.mainFinding: Higher pitches map to lighter stimuli and lower pitches to darker stimuli in non-synesthetes. Ascending melodic intervals mapped to lighter colors. No hue data collected.

systems.AdditionalComment: Confirmed pitch-lightness in non-synesthetes. Larger intervals produced more extreme lightness choices.

systems.name: Mondloch and Maurer Developmental Pitch-Lightness
systems.author: Catherine Mondloch and Daphne Maurer

keyFindings.mainFinding: Pitch-lightness correspondence demonstrated in toddlers, supporting the neonatal synesthesia hypothesis.

systems.AdditionalComment: Supports the hypothesis that pitch-lightness mapping may be innate.

systems.name: Palmer, Schloss, Xu, and Prado-León Emotion-Mediated Study
systems.author: Stephen Palmer, Karen Schloss, Zoe Xu, and Lilia Prado-León

keyFindings.mainFinding: Music-color associations are mediated by emotion rather than direct pitch-hue links.
keyFindings.details: Faster music in major mode → lighter, more saturated, yellower colors. Slower music in minor mode → desaturated, darker, bluer colors.
keyFindings.correlations: r = 0.89–0.99 between emotional profiles of music and chosen colors
keyFindings.crossCultural: Cross-culturally consistent between US and Mexican participants

systems.AdditionalComment: The landmark study demonstrating that music-color associations are mediated by emotion. This is the most parsimonious account for why people associate colors with music.

systems.name: Palmer, Langlois, and Schloss Replication
systems.author: Stephen Palmer, Thomas Langlois, and Karen Schloss

keyFindings.mainFinding: Replicated 2013 findings with 64 controlled single-line Mozart piano melodies. Faster tempo + major mode → saturated, lighter, yellower color choices.

systems.AdditionalComment: Replication of Palmer et al. (2013) with more controlled stimuli.

systems.name: Hamilton-Fletcher et al. Equiluminant Hue Study
systems.author: Giles Hamilton-Fletcher, Christoph Witzel, David Reby, and Jamie Ward

keyFindings.mainFinding: Low frequencies map to blue hues; frequencies above ~800 Hz consistently map to yellow hues. Increased frequency also increased chroma (saturation).
keyFindings.method: Controlled for luminance confounds using equiluminant CIE-Luv colors

systems.AdditionalComment: The strongest evidence for a specific pitch-hue correspondence independent of lightness. However, contradicted by Anikin & Johansson (2019).

systems.name: Whiteford et al. Genre-Dependent Music-Color
systems.author: Kelly Whiteford, Karen Schloss, Nora Helwig, and Stephen Palmer

keyFindings.mainFinding: Loud, distorted music mapped to darker, redder, more saturated colors — mapping onto the red/green hue dimension rather than the yellow/blue dimension found for classical music.

systems.AdditionalComment: Genre-dependence undermines claims of universal pitch-hue correspondence.

systems.name: Anikin and Johansson IAT Pitch-Hue Study
systems.author: Andrey Anikin and Niklas Johansson

keyFindings.mainFinding: When luminance and saturation were properly controlled, no association between pitch and hue was found — except a weak, marginal tendency to match higher pitch with blue (contradicting Hamilton-Fletcher et al.).
keyFindings.confirmedFindings: Pitch mapped reliably to lightness and saturation only.

systems.AdditionalComment: The most comprehensive controlled study. Contradicts Hamilton-Fletcher et al. (2017) on the direction of any marginal pitch-hue effect.

systems.name: Spence and Di Stefano Comprehensive Review
systems.author: Charles Spence and Nicola Di Stefano

keyFindings.mainConclusion: Absence of robust empirical evidence supporting the existence of pitch-hue correspondences in non-synesthetes. Pitch-to-lightness is the only reliable dimension.

systems.AdditionalComment: The most comprehensive modern review. Historical pitch-to-hue mappings all differ from one another, and none has been empirically validated at the population level.

systems.name: Loconsole et al. Tortoise Pitch-Lightness Study
systems.author: Maria Loconsole, Silvia Malaman, Gionata Stancher, and Elisabetta Versace
systems.source: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences (2025)

keyFindings.mainFinding: Higher pitch (700 Hz) associated with white; lower pitch (450 Hz) associated with black. Suggests pitch-lightness correspondence may be phylogenetically ancient.

systems.AdditionalComment: Extends pitch-lightness correspondence to non-mammalian species, suggesting this mapping may be phylogenetically ancient.

systems.name: Sean Day Compiled Synesthesia Databases
systems.author: Sean Day
systems.source: Day (2004–2016), compiled from 130 years of data

keyFindings.trends: A = red (43–44%), I = achromatic (78%), Y = yellow (44%), O = white/achromatic
keyFindings.dayOwnSynesthesia: Timbre-based: piano = sky-blue, tenor saxophone = electric purple, flute = off-white with blue shadings

systems.AdditionalComment: Many synesthetes' pitch-color associations are mediated through letter-name associations (documented since Sachs in 1812), making grapheme-color patterns directly relevant to pitch-color questions.

systems.name: Novich, Cheng, and Eagleman Synesthesia Battery
systems.author: Scott Novich, Shangmin Cheng, and David Eagleman

keyFindings.testableTypes: Music pitch-color (13 piano tones, C4 to C5, each presented 3 times from a palette of 16.7 million colors)
keyFindings.mainFinding: Identified 'coloured music synaesthesias' as one of five distinct subgroups, but did not publish aggregate pitch-to-hue distributions.

systems.AdditionalComment: The largest synesthesia study to date. Aggregate pitch-to-hue distributions were not published, representing a missed opportunity for the field.

systems.name: Gregersen et al. Absolute Pitch and Synesthesia
systems.author: Peter Gregersen et al.

keyFindings.synesthesiaRate: 20.1% reported synesthesia; 84% of those reported pitch-color
keyFindings.exampleMappings: C = royal blue, F = green, G = indigo, A = fuchsia, B = brown, E = red, D = purple
keyFindings.genetics: Shared susceptibility locus on chromosome 6q (peak LOD = 4.68)

systems.AdditionalComment: Demonstrates a strong genetic link between absolute pitch and synesthesia, with shared susceptibility on chromosome 6q.

systems.name: Friedrich Mahling Historical Bibliography
systems.author: Friedrich Mahling
systems.AdditionalComment: Compiled 533 published papers dealing with colored hearing alone — an invaluable historical bibliography.

systems.name: Neil Harbisson Sonochromatic Scale
systems.author: Neil Harbisson

mappings.red: approximately between F and F# (384–718 Hz range)
mappings.system: 360 hues → 360 microtones in one audible octave

systems.AdditionalComment: Harbisson transposes light frequencies 37 octaves lower to produce audible sound via bone conduction. His logarithmic scale maps 360 hues to 360 microtones within one audible octave (384–718 Hz). Standard piano notes fall between microtones. The system is purely physical: direct mathematical transposition with no cultural or harmonic considerations.

systems.name: Chroma-Notes / Boomwhackers Educational System
systems.author: Craig Ramsell
systems.source: Boomwhackers (Craig Ramsell); integrated into Finale, MuseScore, Flat.io, Soundslice
systems.AdditionalComment: The most widely used educational color-note system globally. Chromatic notes use intermediate color-wheel hues. Theoretical basis is pragmatic: 12 chromatic notes mapped to 12 equally-spaced positions around the color wheel, with readability adjustments.

systems.name: Figurenotes Accessibility System
systems.author: Kaarlo Uusitalo and Markku Kaikkonen
systems.source: Resonaari Special Music Center, Helsinki, Finland
systems.AdditionalComment: Developed for accessibility at the Resonaari Special Music Center, Helsinki. Octaves are differentiated by shape (rectangles, circles, triangles), not color. Colors were chosen for maximum visual distinction, not acoustic or synesthetic logic. Now used in Finland, Scotland, Japan, and Estonia.

systems.name: EyeMusic Sensory Substitution Device
systems.author: Sami Abboud, Shlomi Levy-Tzedek, Shachar Maidenbaum, and Amir Amedi
systems.AdditionalComment: Maps color to timbre (not pitch): pitch encodes vertical position on a pentatonic scale, making this a spatial rather than musical color system.

systems.name: Chromatone Open-Source System
systems.author: Denis Starov
systems.AdditionalComment: An online tool mapping A = red (aligning the lowest-frequency visible color with the first-named note), then proceeding chromatically.

systems.name: Fred Collopy 'Three Centuries of Color Scales' Chart
systems.author: Fred Collopy
systems.AdditionalComment: The single most reproduced comparison visualization, showing 13 systems side-by-side as colored bars for all 12 chromatic notes. Chart image at files.rhythmiclight.com/correspondences/colorscales.png.

systems.name: Jörg Jewanski 'Ist C = Rot?' Doctoral Dissertation
systems.author: Jörg Jewanski
systems.AdditionalComment: The definitive historical compilation of color-tone correspondence systems from antiquity through Goethe, containing dozens of specific mapping tables. Foundation for virtually all subsequent historical surveys.

systems.name: Kenneth Peacock 'Instruments to Perform Color-Music'
systems.author: Kenneth Peacock
systems.AdditionalComment: Foundational scholarly reference for color organ instrument history.

systems.name: José Luis Caivano 'Color and Sound: Physical and Psychophysical Relations'
systems.author: José Luis Caivano
systems.AdditionalComment: Provides the key structural analysis of how hue/pitch, luminosity/loudness, and saturation/timbre relate across modalities.

systems.name: Louis Bertrand Castel Ocular Harpsichord
systems.author: Louis Bertrand Castel
systems.source: Castel, L.B. (1725) 'Clavecin pour les yeux'; Franssen (1991); Peacock (1988)
systems.AdditionalComment: First person to build a color organ (clavecin oculaire). Castel proposed that blue was the darkest color and corresponded to C, mapping upward through the spectrum. His system is inverted relative to Newton (who started with red=C). Published in Mercure de France and later in L'Optique des couleurs (1740).

systems.name: George Field Chromatic Equivalents
systems.author: George Field
systems.source: Field, G. (1816) 'Chromatics; or, an Essay on the Analogy and Harmony of Colours'
systems.AdditionalComment: Field followed Newton's spectral ordering (red=C) but applied it to the diatonic scale. His work influenced later color theorists and was one of the most direct applications of Newton's prismatic analogy to music.

systems.name: Alexander Wallace Rimington Colour-Organ
systems.author: Alexander Wallace Rimington
systems.source: Rimington, A.W. (1912) 'Colour-Music: The Art of Mobile Colour'
systems.AdditionalComment: Rimington built a large colour-organ demonstrated at St. James's Hall, London. His mapping follows a strict linear spectral analogy from deep red at C ascending through the spectrum to violet at B. Published his theory in 'Colour-Music' (1912).

systems.name: David A. Wells Proportional Frequency System
systems.author: David A. Wells
systems.source: Wells, D.A. (1980) 'Tonal Design in the Rhetoric of Sound and Light'
systems.AdditionalComment: Wells proposed a proportional mapping between audible and visible frequency ranges. The chromatic scale maps linearly onto the color wheel, with C=red following Newton's tradition. Includes sharp boundaries between semitones.

systems.name: Ralph W. Pridmore Wavelength-Frequency Transposition
systems.author: Ralph W. Pridmore
systems.source: Pridmore, R.W. (1992) 'Music and color: Relations in the psychophysical perspective', Color Research & Application 17(1), 57–61
systems.AdditionalComment: Pridmore used a psychophysically-principled transposition from audible to visible frequencies. He applied a logarithmic scaling to map one octave of pitch onto the visible spectrum. Published in Color Research & Application.

systems.name: Soundmap (Mobile Application)
systems.author: Soundmap developers
systems.source: Soundmap mobile app; Collopy (2009) comparative chart
systems.AdditionalComment: Mobile application that visualizes audio as color in real-time. Uses a standard linear spectral mapping from red (C) through the visible spectrum. Representative of the modern technology implementations that default to Newton-derived spectral mappings.
